analysis.one_liner: Ends a federal tax break for hardrock mines on public land and channels part of the savings into cleaning up abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote, leaving the hardrock mining tax break intact.
analysis.plain_summary: Hardrock miners already get cheap access to federal land under the 1872 mining laws, and on top of that they claim a 'percentage depletion' tax deduction worth a share of the value of every ounce of gold, silver, or copper they pull out. This bill would have ended that tax deduction for mines on federal mining lands or land patented under those laws, and would have put 25 percent of the extra tax revenue into a new fund to seal, regrade, and revegetate abandoned mine sites and treat the water pollution they leave behind.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who stop paying an effective subsidy to companies mining public land; people living near abandoned hardrock mines, whose streams and soils would be reclaimed with the new fund; and the Treasury, which keeps the other 75 percent of the new revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Disallows the percentage depletion deduction for hardrock mines on lands subject to the general mining laws or patented under them, ending what the bill calls a double subsidy on top of cheap public-land access [S3][S2].

Creates an Abandoned Mine Reclamation Trust Fund seeded with 25 percent of the added revenue, available to the Interior Secretary to fill and grade abandoned mine openings, replant eroded lands, control surface subsidence, and treat acid mine drainage [S3].
Targets only sites with no continuing reclamation responsibility under state or federal law and no economically minable minerals, focusing the money on truly orphaned hazards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies — gold, silver, copper, and other metal miners operating on federal mining lands — lose a deduction that has sheltered a percentage of their gross income since 1926, raising their federal taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on public land

drawbacks.text: The tax change could raise costs for domestic metal miners, which supporters of the industry argue risks jobs in mining towns and could shift some production overseas, where environmental rules may be weaker.

Only 25 percent of the new revenue goes to cleanup; the fund covers just a slice of the abandoned-mine problem, excluding coal, fluid minerals, and sites already slated for cleanup under Superfund or uranium tailings laws [S3].
The fund depends entirely on how much extra revenue the repeal actually raises, so cleanup money would fluctuate with metal prices and mining activity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: a tax deduction on public-land mining ends and some money goes to cleaning up hazards the industry left behind. The costs are real but modest — some mining companies pay more, and only a quarter of the savings funds reclamation. On balance this was a targeted subsidy repeal, not a sweeping overhaul of the 1872 mining law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Feingold, Leahy, and Jeffords introduced the bill on January 22, 2001 [S3][S5].
Four senators — two Democrats and two Republicans — signed on as cosponsors, giving it bipartisan but thin support [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003, without the bill ever reaching the floor, so the depletion allowance for hardrock mines on public land remains in the tax code [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies kept their percentage depletion deduction on public-land mines, and taxpayers continued to absorb that cost while abandoned mine sites went unreclaimed.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired successively by Chuck Grassley (R) and Max Baucus (D) during the 107th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or floor action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic lead sponsor plus two Democratic and two Republican cosponsors — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of opposition was never revealed.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper, and other metals on federal mining lands)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped their percentage depletion deduction for mines on public and patented mining lands, ending a tax break layered on top of cheap access to federal minerals. Ordinary taxpayers would have borne less of that subsidy burden.

industries.industry: Mine reclamation and environmental remediation contractors
industries.note: The new trust fund would have paid contractors to seal mine openings, revegetate eroded land, and treat abandoned-mine water pollution — work that also protects nearby residents.
